pages.title: 1. Paleolithic Age (Old Stone Age: ~2 Million BC – 10,000 BC)

content.heading: Lifestyle
content.text: Nomadic hunter-gatherers. No knowledge of agriculture, pottery, or permanent housing.

content.heading: Materials
content.text: Tools were primarily made of unpolished Quartzite stone (Paleolithic humans in India are often called "Quartzite Men").

content.heading: Sub-divisions
content.text:
• Lower Paleolithic: Characterized by hand axes, cleavers, and choppers. Major sites: Soan Valley, Belan Valley (UP), Bori (Maharashtra - earliest evidence of humans in India).
• Middle Paleolithic: Characterized by flake tools (scrapers, borers). Major site: Narmada River Valley (where the Narmada Human skull was found).
• Upper Paleolithic: Characterized by blades and bone tools. Emergence of Homo sapiens. Major sites: Kurnool caves (evidence of fire/ash).

pages.title: 2. Mesolithic Age (Middle Stone Age: ~10,000 BC – 8,000 BC)

content.heading: Lifestyle
content.text: A transitional phase. Hunting and gathering continued, but the domestication of animals began.

content.heading: Tools
content.text: Microliths (miniature stone tools, 1–5 cm long) used as spearheads and arrowheads.

content.heading: Key Sites
content.text:
• Bagor (Rajasthan) and Adamgarh (Madhya Pradesh): Provide the earliest evidence of animal domestication in India.
• Langhnaj (Gujarat): Evidence of microliths and animal bones.
• Mahadaha (UP): Bone artifacts and burials found.

pages.title: 3. Neolithic Age (New Stone Age: ~8,000 BC – 4,000 BC)

content.heading: Lifestyle
content.text: A revolutionary phase marked by settled agriculture, animal husbandry, and village communities.

content.heading: Major Inventions
content.text: The wheel (leading to carts and spinning) and pottery (for storing grains and cooking).

content.heading: Tools
content.text: Polished stone tools, notably stone axes and celts.

content.heading: Key Sites
content.text:
• Mehrgarh (Balochistan): Earliest evidence of agriculture (wheat and barley) and settled life in the Indian subcontinent.
• Burzahom and Gufkral (Kashmir): Known for pit-dwellings and the practice of burying domestic dogs with their masters.
• Chirand (Bihar): Famous for an abundance of tools made from deer antlers and bones.
• Koldihwa (UP): Earliest evidence of rice cultivation.

content.heading: Lifestyle
content.text: The transition from stone to metal. A largely rural/village-based farming economy.

content.heading: Materials
content.text: Simultaneous use of copper (the first metal used by humans) and stone.

content.heading: Pottery
content.text: Widespread use of Black and Red Ware (BRW) painted with white linear designs. Infant mortality was high (evidenced by urn burials).

content.heading: Key Cultures & Sites
content.text:
• Ahar Culture (Rajasthan): Unique because they used mostly copper tools and very few stone tools.
• Malwa Culture (MP): Navdatoli site; yielded the largest variety of food grains. Known for the finest Chalcolithic pottery.
• Jorwe Culture (Maharashtra): Sites like Inamgaon and Daimabad (largest Chalcolithic site). Evidence of social stratification and fortified settlements.

content.heading: Location
content.text: Located in the Vindhya range in Raisen district, Madhya Pradesh. A UNESCO World Heritage Site.

content.heading: Discovery & Time Period
content.text: Discovered by V.S. Wakankar in 1957. The paintings span the Paleolithic, Mesolithic, and historic periods, but the majority belong to the Mesolithic Age.

content.heading: Themes & Colors
content.text: Everyday life, hunting scenes, dancing, animal fights, and family life. Animals like bison, tigers, boars, and elephants are frequently depicted. Natural earth pigments used: Red (hematite) and white were the most common, with occasional use of green and yellow.
